title: More Mating Nets
subtitle: Six more finishing pictures every attacker should own.
goals: Finish with queen-and-pawn and queen-and-knight duos
Convert doubled rooks on the seventh

steps.say: Attacks succeed when you already know the finishing picture. You've met the back rank, Anastasia, Boden, Damiano, Philidor and the Greek Gift — here are six more, each a one-move kill. The pattern to internalize in every case: one piece takes away the flight squares, the other delivers the blow.

steps.prompt: Rook and knight. Mate in one.
hints: Which squares does the g5 knight already control around the black king?
It covers h7 and f7 — so the back rank is the only door left. Slam it.

line.say: The knight seals h7, the king's own g7 pawn blocks his last retreat, and the rook mates on the back rank. Rook + knight is the most common attacking duo in practical chess — this is the picture it aims for.

steps.wrongSay: Count the squares the knight covers, then find the check the king cannot answer.
steps.successSay: Rook mates, knight covers the escape. Whenever you have R+N near a king, look for this.

steps.prompt: Queen and pawn — the humblest support in chess. Mate in one!
hints: The f6 pawn guards g7. A queen that lands there cannot be taken by the king.

line.say: The queen sits right next to the king, protected by a single pawn — and that is the entire mate. Any time you have a pawn on f6 (or h6) against a castled king, the queen is one move from ending the game.

steps.wrongSay: Look for a queen move to a square your pawn already defends.
steps.successSay: A pawn on f6 is worth an attacking piece. Plant one and the queen finishes.

steps.prompt: Rook and bishop, working from opposite ends of the board. Mate in one.
hints: The b2 bishop is aiming down the long diagonal at g7 — so the king cannot step there.
The rook takes the h-file to the back rank: Rh8#.

line.say: The long-diagonal bishop covers g7 from three squares away while the rook delivers on h8 — and Black's own rook on e8 blocks the last escape. Distant bishops are the most-missed defenders AND the most-missed attackers.

steps.wrongSay: The bishop already covers g7 from far away. Which rook check has no answer?
steps.successSay: A bishop on the long diagonal turns a lone rook into a mating attack.

steps.prompt: Queen and knight — the deadliest attacking pair. Mate in one!
hints: The e6 knight covers g7 and f8. That leaves the king exactly nowhere.

line.say: Queen and knight cover squares no other pair can: the knight's protection lets the queen sit right beside the king. This duo is why swapping your knight for a bishop before an attack is so often a mistake.

steps.wrongSay: The knight protects g7. Put the queen there.
steps.successSay: Queen + knight — keep them on the board when you're attacking.

steps.prompt: Two rooks on the seventh — the 'blind swine'. Feed them: mate in one!
hints: The rooks already own the whole seventh rank. The king has no moves at all — he just needs to be checked.
Swing one rook to the back rank.

line.say: Blind swine converted. Doubled rooks on the seventh usually force mate or perpetual by themselves — when you get them there, look for the back-rank switch first.

steps.wrongSay: The seventh rank is already sealed. Deliver the check on the eighth.
steps.successSay: Two rooks on the seventh: get them there and the mate finds itself.

steps.prompt: The king is boxed in by his own rooks. Mate in one — and mind the escape squares!
hints: His rooks block d8 and f8. Only d7, e7 and f7 remain — cover all three at once.
Qe6! — the queen touches every remaining square while checking down the e-file.

line.say: The swallowtail (or 'Gueridon') mate: the queen covers d7, e7 and f7 from one square while the king's own rooks seal the back rank. Crowded kings die of their own furniture — a theme you've now met three times.

steps.wrongSay: Three flight squares, one queen move. Which square touches d7, e7 and f7 together?
steps.successSay: Six new pictures banked. Attacks are pattern recognition — and your library just doubled.
